what_its_for: Loxapine is used to treat schizophrenia, which is a mental health condition that can cause confused thinking, seeing or hearing things that are not there, and unusual beliefs. The inhaled form (Adasuve) is also used to quickly calm agitation in adults with schizophrenia or bipolar disorder.
how_to_take: Loxapine capsules are taken by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the capsule whole — do not crush, chew, or open it. The inhaled powder form (Adasuve) is only given by a healthcare provider in a medical setting and is breathed in through a special inhaler device. Take your medication exactly as your doctor tells you, and do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel better.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it to find the right amount for you. For capsules, the usual starting dose is 10 mg taken twice a day. Your doctor may adjust your dose up to 50 mg per day in the first week, and doses typically range from 60 mg to 100 mg per day. Some people may need up to 250 mg per day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions because your dose is personalized for you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and just take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store loxapine capsules at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the medication away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medication after the expiration date printed on the label. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking loxapine, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness and may cause serious side effects. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medication affects you, because it can cause significant drowsiness. Avoid getting overheated or dehydrated — drink enough fluids, especially in hot weather or during exercise. Be careful when standing up quickly, as loxapine can cause a drop in blood pressure that may make you feel dizzy or faint. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements, because many medications can interact with loxapine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the nearest emergency room if you experience: muscle stiffness, high fever, sweating, fast or irregular heartbeat, or confusion (these may be signs of a rare but serious condition called neuroleptic malignant syndrome); uncontrolled movements of your face, tongue, lips, arms, or legs (this could be a sign of tardive dyskinesia); severe dizziness or fainting; trouble breathing or swallowing; signs of low white blood cell count such as fever, chills, or frequent infections; thoughts of harming yourself or others; or a seizure. Also call your doctor if you notice increased drowsiness, unusual changes in mood or behavior, or any side effects that worry you or do not go away.
when_it_works: You may start to notice some improvement in symptoms such as agitation or anxiety within the first few days of taking loxapine. However, it may take several weeks — usually 2 to 6 weeks — before you feel the full benefit of the medication for symptoms like hallucinations and disorganized thinking. It is important to keep taking your medication every day as prescribed, even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults: Loxapine should be used with great caution in elderly patients, especially those with dementia, as it may increase the risk of serious side effects including stroke and death. Older adults are also more sensitive to dizziness and falls. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Loxapine may cause temporary movement problems or withdrawal symptoms in newborns if taken late in pregnancy. Breastfeeding: It is not known if loxapine passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Loxapine is generally not approved for use in children. Always tell your doctor about all your medical conditions, including heart problems, liver or kidney disease, seizures, difficulty urinating, glaucoma, or low blood pressure, as these may affect how you use this medication.
